To hypnotize someone means to guide them into a special, altered mental state called a trance — a condition where the person is deeply relaxed, their normal busy thoughts are quieted, and their mind becomes unusually open to suggestion. Think of it as putting someone's critical, analytical mind temporarily "on pause," while a deeper, more receptive layer of their mind becomes active and engaged.

The person who does this is called a hypnotist. The person it is done to is said to be hypnotized.
What Actually Happens When Someone Is Hypnotized

When you hypnotize someone, you typically:

  • Relax them deeply — through a calm voice, slow instructions, or guided imagery (like asking them to imagine a peaceful place).
  • Narrow their focus — their attention becomes concentrated, almost like a spotlight in a dark room. Everything outside that spotlight fades away.
  • Increase their suggestibility — they become more willing to accept and act on ideas, instructions, or mental images without their usual resistance or doubt.

The hypnotized person is not unconscious. They are not asleep. They are not under someone else's control the way a robot is controlled. They are aware, but in a deeply focused and receptive state — somewhat like how you feel when you are completely absorbed in a book or a movie and don't notice time passing.
Who Uses This Word and How

1. In medicine and therapy (clinical use)

Therapists and doctors hypnotize patients to help them manage pain, overcome phobias, quit smoking, reduce anxiety, or process traumatic memories. Here, hypnotizing is a legitimate, recognized technique.

"The therapist hypnotized the patient to help him manage chronic pain."

2. On stage and in entertainment (performance use)

Stage hypnotists hypnotize volunteers from the audience and give them entertaining suggestions — like convincing them they are chickens or that they have forgotten their own name. This is the version most people are familiar with from TV and shows.

"The hypnotist hypnotized five people from the crowd, and they all started dancing to music only they could hear."

3. In everyday, figurative language (informal use)

This is the most common way ordinary people use the word in daily life. When something captures your attention so completely and powerfully that you can barely look away or think of anything else, you say it hypnotizes you. You are not literally in a trance — but the effect feels similar. You are dazzled, spellbound, totally absorbed.

"The sunset was so beautiful that it hypnotized everyone on the beach."
"Her voice hypnotized the entire audience."
"I was completely hypnotized by the rhythm of the waves."

This figurative use is extremely common and natural in English.
The Key Distinction: Literal vs. Figurative

• Hypnotizing someone does NOT give you total control over them. A hypnotized person will not do something that goes deeply against their values or beliefs just because they are told to.
  • You cannot hypnotize someone against their will. Cooperation and willingness are important parts of the process.
  • Being hypnotized does not mean you are weak-minded. In fact, people with strong focus and imagination are often easier to hypnotize.
  • It is not the same as being unconscious or asleep. The person usually remembers what happened.

• Hypnotize → base form: "I can hypnotize you."
  • Hypnotizes → third person singular: "She hypnotizes her patients."
  • Hypnotized → past tense / past participle: "He was hypnotized." / "She hypnotized him."
  • Hypnotizing → present participle: "The hypnotizing voice filled the room."
  • Hypnotic → adjective: "a hypnotic gaze", "hypnotic music"
  • Hypnosis → the noun for the state itself: "under hypnosis"
  • Hypnotist → the person who does it
  • Hypnotism → the practice or study of it

• Mesmerize — nearly identical in meaning; used more often in the figurative sense (to captivate)
  • Entrance (verb) — to fill with wonder and hold someone's complete attention
  • Spellbind — to hold someone completely fascinated, as if under a magic spell
  • Captivate — to attract and hold someone's attention powerfully
  • Bewitch — to charm or fascinate someone

All of these share the idea of overpowering someone's attention, but "hypnotize" specifically carries the connotation of a trance-like, deeply focused state — whether literal or figurative.

To hypnotize is to guide someone into a deeply focused, suggestible trance (literally), or — in everyday language — to capture someone's attention so completely that they are spellbound and absorbed (figuratively).
